abstract: This paper examines how downstream competition shapes a manufacturer's decision to adopt a dual‐channel structure—supplying independent retailers via secret two‐part tariff contracts while also operating a direct channel. We show that the shape of the inverse demand function plays a key role in this decision. Under strictly concave demand, expanding total output raises price sensitivity, while the manufacturer responds less aggressively through its direct channel. These effects lead to a sharp price drop, discouraging aggressive retailer behavior and favoring a dual‐channel structure. In contrast, under strictly convex demand, output expansion reduces price sensitivity, and the manufacturer retreats aggressively. The resulting mild price decline leads each retailer to believe that its own output increase has little market impact, encouraging aggressive competition. As a result, with multiple retailers, the manufacturer may avoid supplying the indirect channel even when only two retailers are present. We further show that under the dual‐channel structure, a higher direct‐channel cost can increase consumer surplus by overly shifting output toward the more efficient indirect channel.
title: Monopoly Versus Dual‐Channel Distribution With Multiple Retailers

abstract: In agriculture, production technologies are often characterised by non‐linearities and stochastic dependence between outputs, particularly between desirable and undesirable outputs. This paper combines the copula‐based semi‐parametric framework for modelling heterogeneous dependence with the by‐production stochastic frontier approach and applies it to the analysis of milk production and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The proposed approach models the dependence parameter as a function of farm‐level characteristics, addressing a key limitation of existing by‐production models that assume either no dependence or a constant dependence structure. Applied to panel data on French dairy farms observed from 2018 to 2022, the model jointly estimates technical and environmental inefficiency and their trade‐off. Model selection based on information criteria supports the presence of heterogeneous dependence between the two production frontiers. The results indicate a high level of both technical and environmental performance among French dairy farms and show that farm structure and management significantly influence inefficiency and the strength of the linkage between milk production and emissions.
journal: Australian Journal of Agricultural and Resource Economics
title: Modelling Heterogeneous Dependence in a Copula‐Linked By‐Production Frontier: Evidence From French Dairy Farms

abstract: This paper studies the determinants of anti‐trade attitudes in the European Union. In particular, it investigates how individuals' perceptions of international trade are shaped by the extent and nature of their local communities' integration into international trade. Drawing on trade theory, the paper argues that this relationship varies across groups of individuals that benefit differently from trade. Results show that differences in trade attitudes between low‐ and high‐skilled workers are driven by the labour market consequences of trade, which affect occupational groups and local economies unevenly. By highlighting the interaction between individual occupational characteristics and local trade exposure, the paper contributes to the understanding of the social and territorial determinants of support for international economic integration.
title: Is International Trade Good for You? Individual and Contextual Determinants of Anti‐Trade Attitudes

abstract: Against the background of the global energy transition, China's new energy (NE) industry has experienced a large-scale expansion. The concentrated release of firms' production capacity in the short term has led to structural or temporary supply-demand imbalances within the industry, resulting in mounting debt pressure and intensified default risk. In the face of weakening domestic market demand and escalating international trade frictions, examining the relationship between capacity imbalance and default risk among NE firms is of great significance for deepening the understanding of energy supply chain security. Based on firm-level panel data of NE enterprises from 2009 to 2023, this paper employs a high-dimensional fixed effects model to investigate the impact of capacity imbalance on distance to default. The results show that: (1) capacity imbalance reduces firms' distance to default, thereby increasing default risk; (2) the moderating effect analysis indicates that the traditional current ratio exacerbates default risk under capacity imbalance, while an improvement in fixed asset turnover can alleviate default pressure by optimizing asset allocation efficiency; and (3) capacity imbalance has a stronger effect on increasing default risk among firms with higher fixed asset ratios and state-owned enterprises. This study suggests establishing a dynamic capacity monitoring and risk warning mechanism to promote the healthy and sustainable development of the NE industry.

title: Capacity imbalance and default risk in new energy firms

abstract: The study introduces a scalable textual measure of corporate entrepreneurship disclosure (CED) and establishes its relevance to external credit ratings. CED increases over the sample period and firms with higher semantic CED receive more favorable external credit ratings, although financial constraints weaken this association. Rating agencies discount entrepreneurial activity in financially constrained firms, which reflects their perceived uncertainty about whether these firms can finance ongoing operations while sustaining entrepreneurial activities.
title: Who benefits from Corporate Entrepreneurship Disclosure? Evidence from Credit Ratings

abstract: Federal food distribution programs aim to address food insecurity while supporting farms and food businesses. Many of these programs include small business set-asides designed to improve outcomes for participating firms, yet little evidence exists quantifying their impact on small business performance. We study the Farmers to Families Food Box (FFFB) program, a temporary initiative operated by the U.S. Department of Agriculture from May 2020 to May 2021 that contracted vendors to assemble and deliver food boxes during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using vendor shipment records linked to firm-level employment data from the National Establishment Time Series, we evaluate whether participation in the program affected employment levels of participating small businesses. We estimate a Dynamic Two-Way Fixed Effect Difference-in-Difference model with matched treatment and comparison groups to test for effects on 2020 and 2021 employment levels while accounting for contemporaneous effects of the Payment Protection Program (PPP). Results show that FFFB participation was associated with higher employment among small businesses, with particularly robust evidence for positive effects in 2021. These findings provide some of the first quantitative evidence linking participation in federal food procurement programs to improved small business employment outcomes.
title: Employment effects of the Farmers to Families Food Box program on small businesses

abstract: We study the transmission of macroprudential policy to loan issuance by banks and nonbank financial intermediaries, and the associated real effects on firm-level outcomes including mergers and acquisitions. We use loan-level data from the global syndicated credit market, information on the type of participating lenders between banks and nonbanks, and shocks to regulatory limits to the banks’ ratio on loans-to-deposits (LTD) to document that a LTD policy tightening reduces credit supply by banks and simultaneously shifts financial intermediation to nonbanks. We show that this credit migration is driven by banks facing high pre-regulation LTD ratios and by nonbanks that are less regulated and free from leading the loan arrangements when issuing term loans. We also find evidence that in response to tighter LTD, borrowing firms with stronger nonbank relationships are shielded more by the decline in bank credit with ensuing relative increases in corporate debt, assets, and capital investment. Finally, firms in countries with better access to nonbank credit differentially increase the number of acquisitions they undertake when LTD policy intensifies.
title: Limits to LTD, loan supply, and real effects: Banks vs. nonbanks

abstract: Which facts about households’ inflation expectations are universal across countries and demographic groups? Using homogeneous survey data from 32,000 respondents in 32 countries. We find substantial heterogeneity in inflation perceptions and expectations: older, male, and economically literate respondents report lower values, while unemployed and impatient respondents higher values. Yet, we detect striking similarity in how perceptions translate into expectations across demographic groups and countries. Inflation narratives also differ sharply: Europeans emphasize geopolitical shocks and supply disruptions, whereas respondents in high-inflation countries blame central banks. Support for non-standard central-bank mandates also varies systematically. Respondents whose preferred mandates differ from those they perceive central banks to pursue have higher inflation expectations and lower trust.
title: Inflation, households, and central banks around the world

abstract: Populism may not only have contemporary but also long-term effects on the macroeconomy. Using data for advanced economies and emerging markets since 1960, this column explores the historical links between populist regimes, fiscal monetisation, and inflation, and how these links affect monetary policy in the 21st century. Historically, left-leaning populist regimes are linked to increases in central bank lending to the central government. In turn, central bank lending is associated with marked increases in inflation. Today, central banks with a history of deficit monetisation and left-wing populist regimes respond more strongly to deviations of inflation expectations from target, suggesting they still need to signal their independence more forcefully.
abstract_zh: 民粹主义不仅可能对宏观经济产生当代影响，还可能产生长期影响。本文利用1960年以来发达经济体和新兴市场的相关数据，探讨民粹主义政权、财政货币化与通货膨胀之间的历史联系，以及这些联系如何影响21世纪的货币政策。从历史上看，左倾民粹主义政权与中央银行对中央政府贷款的增加相关联。反过来，中央银行贷款又与通货膨胀的显著上升相关。如今，那些有赤字货币化历史和左翼民粹主义政权背景的中央银行，对通胀预期偏离目标的反应更为强烈，这表明它们仍需更有力地彰显其独立性。
authors: Luis I. Jácome, Nicolas Magud, Samuel Pienknagura, Martín Uribe
title: Fiscal populism and monetary policy rules
title_zh: 财政民粹主义与货币政策规则

abstract: Innovation has increasingly become a team activity, while inventors have become more concentrated in large firms. This column argues that these trends are closely connected. Team production creates genuine scale advantages in innovation, but can also lead the competitive economy to concentrate inventive activity too heavily in large firms because firms do not internalise knowledge spillovers.
abstract_zh: 创新日益成为一项团队活动，而发明者也越来越集中于大企业。本专栏认为，这两种趋势密切相关。团队生产在创新中创造了真正的规模优势，但也可能导致竞争性经济将发明活动过度集中于大企业，因为企业并未将知识溢出内部化。
authors: Seula Kim, Jane Olmstead-Rumsey, Honghao Wang
title: Ideas and firm dynamics when it takes two to tango
